title: Justice

lines: ONLY SOME OF IT IS MONEY.
cards: Rent. A phone bill. A borrowed book still on your shelf.

A friend who covered lunch last time. A teacher, years back, who believed in you before anyone else did and never heard you say so. Make a list of what you owe and it gets long fast, and only some of it is money.
Christian teachers took up an old, plain definition of justice: giving each their due. Not revenge, not a courtroom drama. Just the steady work of making sure everyone gets what is theirs.

teach.b: Paul comes close to that definition in his letter to the Romans: "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour." Taxes and fees, yes.
But also respect, and honor. Some debts are paid in money and some in thanks, and Paul counts both.
Proverbs adds the timing: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it." If you can pay it now, the delay itself is a small injustice.
Then the prophets widen the frame from my bills to a whole society. Micah asks what the Lord requires, and the first answer is "to do justly." In Hebrew, that's to do mishpat, justice.

teach.h: LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.
teach.b: Amos, as day 484 heard, pictures it as something that should never dry up: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." A river, not a single payment.
Justice keeps flowing toward whoever is owed, especially the people easiest to overlook. And right after the list of dues, Paul says one more thing: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another."
Pay every debt you can, he says, except one.

teach.h: THE ONE DEBT THAT STAYS OPEN.
teach.b: The debt of love stays open. You never get to mark it paid and walk away. Justice gives each their due.

how: Christian moral teaching names justice among the cardinal virtues; churches teach it through paying fair debts and wages, giving thanks and respect, and working for the poor and overlooked, drawing on Micah 6:8 and the prophets.

o: treating everyone exactly the same in every way
giving each their due, in money, honor and thanks
punishing wrongdoers so they get what they deserve

p: let judgment run down as waters

s: justice is only about courts and punishment
it's giving each their due: money, respect, honor, thanks.
Paul lists honor among the debts we owe
Romans 13:7 puts honor and respect on the list beside taxes and fees.
Paul says to pay off every debt, love included, until you owe nothing
"owe no man any thing, but to love one another." that debt stays open.

games.q: you've owed someone a thank-you for years. it's in your power to say it today, but it feels awkward after so long. what does Proverbs say?
o: withhold not good when it's in your power to do it.
it's too late; let it go.
games.why: "withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it."

practice: Let your mind walk slowly through your people and your week, a bill you've been putting off, something borrowed, an apology, a thank-you someone has never heard, and choose one debt, in money or in thanks, that it's in the power of your hand to pay.
Hold it clearly. If you pray, you can ask for help to pay it.

wordCard.voice: Justice. Giving each their due, in money, in honor, in thanks. In the Hebrew of the prophets, mishpat.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, judgment; Micah's 'to do justly' is to do mishpat.

carryVoice: Your line: each their due. The book on the shelf counts too. See you tomorrow.
